# vc-x1-messages v0.3.3

Messages for the vc-x1 family. The open threads are the inbox, the history is the archive.

One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A thread is
one file, appended by everyone who takes part in it, so reading a conversation is reading one
file, and a search for a message's id returns everything ever said under it. Every member's
`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.

## Terminology

Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
under it.

- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
  in any open thread.
- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
  eye, since the position already says it.
- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
  the close.
- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

## Specimen

`open/m-41.md`, opened by abc to def and ghi, answered by both, and complete: ghi's line at 1
and def's at 2 are above 0, the line naming them, and abc's `done` at 3 is above 1 and 2, the
lines naming abc. `threads` holds 41 or more. Line 2 has a body, `open/m-41-2.md` beside it,
shown after it.

```

- m-41-0 2026-09-09T16:00:00Z from abc to def,ghi hello
- m-41-1 2026-09-09T16:05:42Z from ghi to abc hi
- m-41-2 2026-09-09T16:09:12Z from def to abc [hey, and the cycle that answers it](m-41-2.md)
- m-41-3 2026-09-09T16:12:30Z from abc done

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.

  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,

the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

# m-15-0 a clone per member, the remote as the mutex

Wink's idea, 2026-11-17, discussed in a zc-ring-x1 session and sent here because the work is
vc-x1's: the messages repo is a data base, not a dual repo, so the protocol change and the tool
that runs it belong in vc-x1. These are findings, not a decision, and Wink moves the discussion
to vc-x1.

## The idea

Each member clones the messages repo into its own workspace at `.family-messages`, instead of
every member sharing one clone at `../vc-x1-messages`.

- No ownership: no `owner` file, no take and release, and no human clearing a take left by a
  session that died.
- The same path for every member, so `[family] messages` reads alike everywhere.
- Other machines can take part, which the README's "No second machine" rules out today.
- A workspace no longer depends on a sibling directory existing.

## The finding

A clone per member removes the local mutex but not its job, the allocation of ids. Two clones
can both read `threads` as 14 and open thread 15, or both append line 3 to one thread. The
remote can take the job, and the thread files stay exactly as they are: one file per thread,
numeric ids, and the `threads` counter. Only the write procedure changes:

1. Fetch and move to the remote's `main`.
2. Read messages, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
3. Append the line, or open the thread and bump `threads`, commit, and push.
4. A rejected push: drop the commit, return to step 1, and write again.

The remote accepts one push on top of a given commit, so two members never both land the same
id. A line is a pure append and its number is its position, so a retry is a rewrite and never a
merge, and nothing conflicts. The README's "an id is final only once pushed" becomes the whole
allocation rule.

## What it costs

- Every write is a commit and a push. A line is not written until it is pushed, so "an
  uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a pushed one" goes, and each member's
  `custom.md` needs a standing permission for these pushes, as for the fetch.
- No offline writes. A line can be drafted without the remote, not numbered.
- A retry may be a rethink. A line that arrived in the same thread is read before the write is
  made again, which is what step 2 is for.
- A body file is renamed on a retry, its name carrying the line's number. Mechanical, and a
  `vc-x1` subcommand could run the whole loop.
- The nested repo: `.family-messages/` goes into each work-repo's `.gitignore`, an agent-repo
  inside the workspace must not pick it up either, and `rg` from the workspace root skips a
  dot-directory without `--hidden`.

## What gets easier

The version commit. With nothing unpushed counting as written, it is one more push like any
other, and "every member's last push already in `main@origin`" holds by construction.

## Alternatives looked at and passed over

- One file per line, with member-scoped ids, `open/m-12/zc-ring-x1-1.md`: conflict-free with no
  retry, but the numbers no longer order a thread and a conversation is no longer one file. Wink
  was not taken with it.
- Member-scoped ids in the one file, merged by git's union merge: loses "line `<num>` is file
  line `<num>` plus two", and jj does not honour git merge attributes.
- One file per member per thread: reading a conversation means interleaving files.

Each buys concurrent offline writes, which we think the family's traffic does not need.

## Open

- A `vc-x1` subcommand for the loop, fetch, append, commit, push, retry, and whether `vc-x1
  init` makes the clone.
- Whether the clone is plain git or jj-colocated.
- It is a protocol version bump, and the cutover retires `owner` and the shared clone.

entries the dead-end filed, **feat: a rung's state is recorded in TODO.md**, **feat: a closing names
its shape, and its target once**, and **feat: a dead-end lands on a target or a tag**. vc-x1 infers
a cycle's commits from bookmark reachability, so a set-aside bookmark corrupted the ladder and the
commit count twice. `cycle --commit` writes the next rung `(current)`, a prediction. And a cycle
stopped early has no durable end, its agent commits' `ochid:` trailers left naming work commits no
pushed ref keeps. One cycle, its rungs below, wink's "we'll see how it goes".

- **The principle.** The repo holds what happened, and `TODO.md` holds where the cycle is going and
...
| 2 | `--close --multi-step --dead-end --tag [<name>] [--push]` | the dead-end tag | `--open --from <target>` | no |
| 3 | `--close --multi-step --dead-end --no-tag` | nothing, until a tag is pushed | `--open --from <target>` | yes |
| 4 | nothing committed | nothing needed | `--open` | no |
| 5 | outside the tool: `jj abandon`, a bookmark deleted | none | anything | cannot ask |

- **The tags.**
  - The version tag, `m-14`'s ask: `--land <target>` tags the commit the target moves to
    `v<version>`, read by `[version]`'s `file` and `pattern`, `[land] tag = "v{version}"` setting
    the form. `--no-tag` skips it, a tag at the same commit is a no-op, one at another commit is
    refused naming both, and a workspace with no `[version]` gets none, said. A landed dead-end is
    tagged too, its version having moved forward.
  - Tags are lightweight, made by jj-lib with no git spawn, the tagged commit's title saying what it
    is.
  - The dead-end tag is named `dead-end-<ts>`, `<name>`, or `<name>-<ts>`, `<ts>` UTC to the
    millisecond in ISO 8601's basic form, `20261116T215837.123Z`, since a ref holds no `:`. A name
    taken, locally or on the remote, is refused. `--tag-dead-end <rev> [<name>]` tags a closed
...
    on the dead-end, which lands it unasked.
  - `--push-dead-end`, wink's lean, `--push` kept so a dead-end is reviewed before it is published.
  - Annotated tags, which jj-lib does not make, so a git spawn against `clippy.toml`'s register.
- **Carried and left out.**
  - A block per rung is a trial, wink's "see how the noise feels".
  - The dead-end's rungs 1 and 2 hold the `(done)`-only ladder and its tests to take back, and its
    closing rung says what today's dead-end path taught. `m-13` and `m-14` are told when it lands.
  - Out of it, each its own entry: **feat: a short form for ending a cycle**, **feat: a cycle takes
    an added bookmark**, and **A parked head is durable and continues on any machine**.

content.content:
vc-x1 0.85.29+99bd1a4be41e

Commit the working copies as a rung's pair, one commit per repo of a
dual workspace, each stamped with the other's change id, and with
--push publish it in the same invocation, as `vc-x1 push` would.

The diff and the description are reviewed before the commit, so the
push publishes what was reviewed. It stays on the machine unless
--push asks, for a look at it by `vc-x1 show -s both @-` before
`vc-x1 push`. --local says so outright.

-r REV is the commit the description is for: `@` by default,
committed as the working copy, else `@-` or any draft below it,
described in place with no new commit and its trailer stamped, so a
commit made by hand becomes a rung's. A draft below `@-` is kept
local, since push publishes `@-`. The old positional is refused,
naming -r.

A cycle's opening, rungs, closing, and Land are `vc-x1 cycle`'s, which
makes its commits by this command's code. --opening, --closing, and
--land are retired, each refused naming its stage.

-s is required: `b` makes both commits now, `w` the work half with
the agent half left to push, `a` the agent repo alone, unpaired, with
no trailer, and `p` a plain repo with no trailer. -R is optional and
says where. --body is the text, or @PATH to read it from a file.

With `[version] file` and `pattern` in the config, a work commit that
changes no line of the file starting with the pattern is refused, a
rung bumping the version, and --same-version commits it as it is.

-s a --covers REVSET makes the agent commit a cycle's rungs share:
one `ochid:` per work commit REVSET names, oldest first, the revset
taken as written, no base assumed, and each must name the agent @.

Usage: vc-x1 commit [OPTIONS] --scope <SCOPE> --title <STR> --body <STR|@PATH>

Options:
  -r, --revision <REV>
          The commit the description is for: `@` by default, committed as the
          working copy; `@-` or any draft below it is described in place with no
          new commit, its trailer stamped, so a commit made by hand becomes a
          rung's

  -V, --version...

headings the record needs, and a file there is kept. Every check is

content.content:
## Suffix scheme

The cycle (opening -> commits -> closing, per the [Cycle protocol](../AGENTS.md#cycle-protocol))
encodes each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a
Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is not
a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries neither a
number nor a version (see [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: the commits between
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0` and
starts at `-1` (its first commit). A single-step cycle is one commit, the Close-out, and carries the
bare `X.Y.Z` ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0`
step without renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10`: commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its commits between
- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the step),
so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference above, every
commit carries a distinct version. The bump is the project's, by its own tool, and `vc-x1` never
writes a version: with `[version] file` and `pattern` in the config it refuses a commit that
leaves the version's line unchanged, and `--same-version` commits it as it is.

content.text:
I agree. I'm reading "one line" as "one commit". If you meant something else, say so.

**Why it fits:**
- The rules define a proposal as "one set of diffs". A single commit taking `-N` to a bare `v0.3.1` is that set exactly, and an adopter reviews it as one diff.
- Every change to the rules then lands earlier, in its own cycle, each bumping the draft (`-19`, `-20`, …). The proposal itself adds no new rules. It writes the gathered `####` changes and their whys into the entry, bumps the agent-files version, and sends the message.
- The prep cycles get ordinary Conventional titles. That takes care of the warning without exempting anything from it.

**What it changes:**
- **This cycle** should restart as something like **feat: a link stays on one line**. It's `feat` because `check anchors` gains a warning; since it's a style to strive for, it warns rather than refuses. Its agent-files rung bumps to `-19`.
- **The Todo headings** named `agent-files(proposal): …` that are really prep get renamed to their Conventional form. That's this one, **dry runs interleave**, and **vc-x1 is the interface, jj the engine**. Only **agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1** keeps the proposal form.
- **Your two decisions become prep cycles:**
  - `custom.md` is committed: the rule changes, vc-x1 un-ignores and commits its own, and `AGENTS.md > custom.md` stops calling it "one machine's paths".
  - vc-x1 by default and jj when needed: the **jj, not git** rule is reworded.
  - They might share a cycle or the link cycle, but kept apart each diff stays small.
- **The proposal commit's own title** is the one place the non-Conventional form stays, and it gets that one warning. Alternatively, something like `docs: propose agent-files v0.3.1` keeps even that conventional. I lean towards keeping `agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1`, since adopters search for that form.

**One cost:** the proposal commit is big, all the whys written into one entry. It's doc-only, though, and its review is the convergence review the family does anyway.

**Where things stand, untouched since last time:**
- The cycle is started under the old title, with nothing committed. A restart is `jj op restore` to before `plan start`, then `plan start` again under the new title.
- The messages commit is still local and not pushed.

The plain version: yes, make the proposal one commit, run each rule change before it as an ordinary cycle, and restart this one as **feat: a link stays on one line**. I'll wait for your go before changing anything.

content.content:
## In Progress

A cycle's record has one home at a time, and while the cycle runs this is it. The block's shape is
the specimen in [cycle-model.md](agent-data/cycle-model.md), and the rules are in [The In Progress
block](agent-data/notes.md#the-in-progress-block).

### feat: a link stays on one line

#### Problem

(wink + agent, 2026-11-25, from **feat: init copies a file set and finishes what it starts**) A
link's text wraps with the prose around it, `[Working` ending one line and `practices](...)`
opening the next, as 128 links do today, 65 of them in the agent-files. A search for the link's
text then misses it, a previewer may not join it, and `check anchors` has a bug of its own for a
citation after a wrapped code span. Wink read one in `custom.md` and was not sure it was valid.

- **Solution**: a rule in `prose.md`'s Line widths, a check, and a sweep.
  - A link, text and destination, is never split across lines.
  - A link that does not fit the line within the prose width starts the next line.
  - A link longer than the width alone is the exception to it, as a URL is already.
  - `check anchors` refuses a link that spans a line.
- **Acceptance check**: `check anchors` over the agent-files reports no link spanning a line, and
  refuses a file given one.
- **The short lines are a fair trade** (wink, 2026-11-25): a line broken early before a link is
  ragged in the source alone, never rendered.
- **What follows a moved link**, open: the agent reads the rule as letting the text after a link
  go on along its line while it fits, the line after taking it only when the link fills its own.
  Wink's "on the next line by itself" may mean a moved link is always alone on its line.
- **The sweep**: the agent-files by the cycle that makes the rule, `TODO.md` (32), `notes/` (16),
  `README.md` (11), and the skeleton's templates (2) as a cycle touches each or by a sweep of its
  own, as the semicolons went. `custom.md`'s one was joined by hand, the file being local.
- Closes **validate-anchors finds a citation that follows a wrapped code span** by rule.
- To be carried by **agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1**.

#### Solution

_To write._

#### Acceptance check

_To write._

#### Deliberation

_None._

#### Problem

link's text wraps with the prose around it, `[Working` ending one line and `practices](...)`

citation after a wrapped code span. Wink read one in `custom.md` and was not sure it was valid.

  - A link, text and destination, is never split across lines.
  - A link that does not fit the line within the prose width starts the next line.
  - A link longer than the width alone is the exception to it, as a URL is already.
  - `check anchors` refuses a link that spans a line.

  refuses a file given one.

  ragged in the source alone, never rendered.

  go on along its line while it fits, the line after taking it only when the link fills its own.

  writes again. `owner` and the shared clone retire, a version bump of the protocol.

  one push refused, and the retry lands both lines numbered in order with no conflict.

  git or jj-colocated, and each write a push, so each member's `custom.md` needs a standing
  permission for them.
- The body: `../vc-x1-messages/open/m-15-0.md`. A line in `m-15` gives this entry's sha-link once
  it is pushed.

import re,glob,subprocess
files=subprocess.run(['jj','file','list'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.split()
md=[f for f in files if f.endswith('.md')]
def count(f):
    n=0; fence=False
    for l in open(f):
        if l.lstrip().startswith('```'): fence=not fence; continue
        if fence: continue
        l=re.sub(r'`[^`]*`','',l)
        for m in re.finditer(r'\]\(|\]\[',l):
            depth=0; ok=False
            for c in reversed(l[:m.start()]):
                if c==']': depth+=1
                elif c=='[':
                    if depth==0: ok=True;break
                    depth-=1
            if not ok: n+=1
    return n
tot={}
for f in md:
    c=count(f)
    if c: tot[f]=c
af=sum(v for k,v in tot.items() if k=='AGENTS.md' or k.startswith('agent-data/'))
print('agent-files',af)
for k in sorted(tot,key=lambda k:-tot[k])[:25]: print(tot[k],k)
print('total',sum(tot.values()))
EOF

#### Solution

A style to strive for, not a requirement (wink, 2026-11-27): a rule in `prose.md`'s Line widths,
a count in `check anchors` that never fails it, and the agent-files swept, as the set this rule
joins.

- The rule: a link, its text and destination, inline or reference-style, stays on one line. One
  that does not fit within the prose width starts the next line, the text after it going on along
  that line while it fits, and one longer than the width alone is the exception, as a URL is.
- The check: `check anchors` finds a link whose text began on an earlier line, a `](` or `][`
  with no `[` of its own before it on the line, and reports it as a style site, not a finding.
  Its summary gains `N link(s) span a line`, each site at `-v`, and the exit status is unchanged.
- The sweep: the agent-files, 69 links today, re-wrapped by hand. The rest, 64 in `TODO.md`,
  `notes/`, `README.md`, and the skeleton's templates, re-wrap when a cycle touches them, the
  Line widths rule's "no mass sweeps".
- The agent-files version bumps to `v0.3.1-19`, a prep cycle of **agent-files(proposal):
  v0.3.1**.

#### Acceptance check

`vc-x1-dev check anchors --file` over `AGENTS.md` and each `agent-data/*.md` reports `0 link(s)
span a line` and passes, a scratch file holding one wrapped inline link and one wrapped reference
link reports `2 link(s) span a line` and still passes, and the validate task passes.

#### Deliberation

- **A count, not a warning per link**: 133 wrapped links today, so a warning each would bury every
  validate's output until a sweep nobody is asked to make. The summary keeps the number in view and
  `-v` names the sites.
- **What follows a moved link** (open in the entry): the agent's reading, the text after the link
  going on along its line, since a link alone on every line it starts would make the ragged source
  wink accepted ragged far more often. Wink's to confirm at the plan's review.
- **Agent-files swept, the rest by touch**: the agent-files are what the proposal hands the family,
  and the set should show the rule it states. Elsewhere Line widths' "no mass sweeps" holds.
- **The wrapped code span stays a bug**: **validate-anchors finds a citation that follows a
  wrapped code span** is a false finding about code spans, not links, so this rule does not close
  it, where the entry said it would. Whether code spans join the rule is wink's to say.
- **Generated text**: `vc-config.md` is built from the schema and carries one wrapped link, so it
  re-wraps when its generator is next touched, not by hand.

#### Rungs

The rung subsections, in the ladder's order. The ladder itself is in `zTOC.md > ## Ladder`.

content.content:
## Tasks

The project's tasks, in the order a change uses them. A change is made as a
[cycle](AGENTS.md#terminology): one commit, or a ladder of commits each called a rung, made on a
bookmark of its own and joined to `main` at the end, the Land. A task is named by its first column,
the name the agent-files use for it.

- Dev and release: the dev build is the quick debug one, for trying a change while it is made, and
  the release build is the optimized one installed as `vc-x1` at Land.
- The commands are the workspace's own `cargo xtask`, the `xtask/` package, which needs nothing
  installed: `cargo xtask -h` lists its tasks, and `cargo xtask completions` explains the shell
  alias, `cx` here, and its completion. Its settings are `Cargo.toml`'s
  `[workspace.metadata.xtask]`.

| Task | What it does | When | Command |
|---|---|---|---|
| bump | sets the version in `Cargo.toml` and refreshes `Cargo.lock`, `X.Y.Z-N` for a cycle's Nth commit and the bare `X.Y.Z` for its last ([Suffix scheme](agent-data/versioning.md#suffix-scheme)) | first, at each commit of a cycle | `cargo xtask bump next`, or `bump X.Y.Z` |
| validate | formats the code, runs the lints, and runs every test, the fixture tests included | before each review, and before every commit | `cargo xtask validate` |
| validate fast | runs the binaries' unit tests only, changing no file | while a review iterates | `cargo xtask validate --fast` |
| test | builds and runs the tests named | to run one test, or the tests matching a filter | `cargo test [<filter>]` |
| clippy | runs the lints, a warning failing it | to see the lints alone | `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` |
| build | builds the dev binary, `target/debug/vc-x1`, with the commit it was built from | to build the change without running it | `cargo xtask build` |
| run | builds the dev binary, then runs it with the arguments, no `--` needed | to try the change | `cargo xtask run <args>` |
| install | builds the dev binary, then copies it into `~/.cargo/bin` as `vc-x1-dev`, beside the installed `vc-x1` | after each rung's commit, and to try the change from any directory | `cargo xtask install` |
| install release | builds the release binary and copies it into `~/.cargo/bin` as `vc-x1`, printing its version | at Land | `cargo xtask install --release` |

Each building task takes `--release` or `--profile NAME`, a `Cargo.toml` profile, dev by default,
and `--bin NAME` for another binary. vc-x1's own `validate`, `build`, `run`, and `install` are
deprecated, each warning and naming its task, and a later release refuses them.
